Proposes an evaluation method; secondary: Compares — AsynCodeBench, a dependency-centric benchmark for asynchronous multi-agent software engineering (19 tasks from 16 repositories, 52 directed dependencies with executable Dependency Checkers) with metrics ADPR and DRS; compares five execution protocols across ten open-weight models

No SDD approach. Five execution protocols (multi-agent workflows) on the OpenHands harness (version Not stated): SINGLE (one agent), SERIAL (specialists with producer-to-consumer handoffs), ASYNC-PRIVATE (concurrent specialists in private workspaces), ASYNC-MANAGER-RO (read-only manager coordinates), ASYNC-MANAGER (manager with bounded repair). Ten open-weight models: Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.5-27B, Qwen3.6-27B, Qwen3.8-27B, Qwen3-Coder-Next (FP8), DeepSeek-V4-Flash (0731), Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, Muse-Glimmer-30B, GLM-4.7-Flash, Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B

Not an approach. Task package: fixed repository revision, answer-free task instruction, scoped writable paths, task-specific pytest evaluator; dependency graph (defined before evaluation) and Dependency Checkers (upstream, downstream, integrated); manager may inspect task specification, dependency graph, artifacts and checker diagnostics

Per protocol: SINGLE solves the whole task; SERIAL: upstream specialist, integration, then downstream specialist; ASYNC-PRIVATE: concurrent specialists, scope validation, deterministic integration in dependency order; manager variants add planning, feedback, scoped follow-up attempts and (ASYNC-MANAGER) scoped repair patches after integration; checkpoints of the integrated workspace recorded
None during runs (manager is an LLM agent). Humans only in benchmark construction: three reviewers validate tasks and each dependency edge

ADPR (Asynchronous Dependency Pass Rate: share of dependencies satisfied in the final integrated workspace); DRS (normalized Dependency Resolution Step: first checkpoint at which a dependency passes; 1 = never); cumulative dependency closure over normalized logical steps ('hopping window'); Pearson/Spearman correlation between Test Pass Rate and ADPR

Automatic: task-specific pytest evaluators and executable Dependency Checkers run on integrated-workspace checkpoints; token counts as reported by the harness. Dependency graphs and tasks validated manually by three reviewers

Tasks: 19 AsynCodeBench tasks. Configurations: 5 protocols x 10 models (40 multi-agent model-protocol configurations plus SINGLE). Constant: task package, OpenHands harness, task-specific Docker environment, same decomposition for SERIAL vs ASYNC-PRIVATE. Baseline: SINGLE (one agent per model). Acceptance: pytest evaluators and pre-defined Dependency Checkers. Repetitions: not stated (one outcome per model-task-protocol). Human intervention: none

Six of ten models improve over SINGLE under their best multi-agent protocol (+7.8 to +22.7%), four do not (e.g. Qwen3.8-27B 93.6% -> 86.7%, DeepSeek-V4 93.6% -> 89.9%). Test Pass Rate and ADPR imperfectly associated under ASYNC-MANAGER-RO (Pearson r = 0.617, Spearman rho = 0.613); 32 outcomes with >=80% Test Pass but <50% ADPR. No protocol improves ADPR for all models (Qwen3.6-27B: -14.9% ASYNC-PRIVATE to +26.3% ASYNC-MANAGER). Multi-agent protocols cost more tokens; Pareto frontiers differ under the two quality metrics for 5 of 10 models. No significance tests

Partly: dependency-level metrics distinguished protocols and models and exposed failures hidden by test pass rates, but repeatability not assessed (single run, no variance). Limitations of the comparison method not stated by the authors

No limitations section. Gaps stated: multi-agent systems lack a direct measure of collaboration; task-level outcomes conflate coding ability with coordination; stronger standalone coding does not translate into stronger collaboration; timing of dependency resolution (hopping window) is a dimension of collaboration capability
